responseSet.title: Psychotherapy with Severely Deprived Children: Eileen
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Psychotherapy with Severely Deprived Children: Eileen

Lisa Miller

Lisa Miller

120, Belsize Lane
London N.W.3.

Lisa Miller  

My aim in this paper is to produce some evidence to support the contention that a child who has suffered a severe degree of maternal deprivation can make use of therapy. In doing this I have tried to describe what seems to me to be the kind of world this particular child inhabits as a result of her early deprivation, and to say something about the difficulties consequent on a deprived start to life — the difficulties for the child, and the difficulties for those in charge of her.

My patient, Eileen, with whom I began work in November 1975 when she was 14, underwent what is perhaps the plainest sort of early deprivation that we are likely to come across. There was no single individual care-taking person in her life: she was in the care of the local authority from birth. Her mother is reported to have been of sub-normal intelligence, and she has never had any contact with Eileen and her twin brother; their father has maintained a very desultory contact. Not only were the twins born to a life with no mother, but they were also premature by two months. This meant that they spent a long while in incubators. Presumably their survival was a matter of touch and go; and they remained weakly babies, ill and in hospital on and off for their first two years. I have deliberately avoided writing about Eileen's twin; I have been able to do this because the twins do not seem to have developed the kind of special relationship which the word ‘twins’ generally calls to mind. I can make various conjectures about why they did not: among them is the fact that at the outset in a hospital nursery they neither had to contend with trying to share a single mother, nor to be aware of the other twin in particular when there were other babies in the ward.

Since the age of two, Eileen has had unusually continuous care, first at a residential nursery where the Matron took a great interest in her and subsequently at a Children's Home where the same Housemother has been in charge ever since Eileen arrived at the age of six. Indeed, Eileen's life has been free from the shocking disasters which often crowd the files of children who end up in care. People have tried to take seriously the task of bringing her up; her own Social Worker is of some years’ standing; her school did all in its power to be helpful. The abiding question is why Eileen has been able to make so little use of what has been offered her, and the answer probably lies, I think, in her infancy.

[[RunningHead]]

Communication and Interpretation in the Opening Phase — Illustrated from the Analysis of an Eight-Year-Old Boy11

Elizabeth Daunton

Elizabeth Daunton

2300 Overlook
Cleveland Heights
Ohio 44106

Elizabeth Daunton  

The theme of the opening phase of treatment has rich associations and raises challenging questions. Historically, analysts recall Anna Freud's (1926) picture of the contrasting attitudes of adult and child at the beginning of treatment. Hoffer (1935) described the unfolding work in the introductory phase of a child analysis and discussed some of the boundary marks of this phase. The modifications in Anna Freud's thinking about the technique of a preparatory period which produce in the child “the missing willingness and readiness” (1926-1946) (p. 5), are well known. They stemmed from her full exporation of defense mechanisms and their relationship to the affects disturbing to the ego. Ways for the analyst to meet the resistances of the opening phase, by approaching warded off affects through the recognition of anxiety, have been discussed and illustrated by Anna Freud (1936, 1946), Berta Bornstein (1945, 1949), and Frankl and Hellman (1962).

While techniques have changed, the analyst's attention in the opening phase is still directed towards the areas identified in Anna Freud's first lecture (1926). These include the child's insight into his problems and his ability to turn the decision for analysis from one taken by others into his own. It is still relevant for the child analyst to trace the steps leading to the decision and to study the dynamic and economic changes in the patient which signal the end of the opening phase. We may now say that this ability makes the “treatment or working alliance” possible while recognizing that this alliance will undergo many vicissitudes (Novick, 1970). It is meaningful for the analyst to trace the steps leading to greater autonomy in the patient as well as to study the dynamic and economic changes which signal the end of the opening phase.

In this paper I shall suggest that particular forms of interpretation predominate in the opening phase, paving the way for a different form at its close. The special features of work with parents during this phase will be considered. The first two and a half months of work with Dan provide the main focus for discussion of these issues.

[[RunningHead]]

Psychotherapy with Severely Deprived Children: Keith

Pamela Berse

Pamela Berse

120, Belsize Lane
London N.W.3.

Pamela Berse  

Keith was abandoned at birth by a mother who herself had been abandoned. Little is known about his infancy, the first 16 months of which were spent in a residential nursery, except that he was said to have screamed incessantly. He was fostered for a year with a couple who had three children of their own, but as it became increasingly evident that Keith was half coloured, the father of the family rejected him. Keith lived in a Children's Home until a second attempt was made to foster him when he was four years’ old, but this broke down only five months later due, it was said, to the bitter jealousy of other children in the foster home. So Keith returned to the Children's Home and began school just one month later.

Not surprisingly, the headmistress of his infant school found him “anti-social and generally destructive, unable to make contact with children or adults, frustrated by the slightest set-back, and usually alone”. Keith was referred to the Tavistock at this time, but psychotherapy was not recommended. Rather it was felt that support should be given to the people who were trying to care for him at home and school. They were patient and dedicated in their efforts to help him. Miss A., his new house mother, who has remained a constant figure in his life, tried to accept his babyish behaviour and carried him everywhere for months. But she was frightened and disturbed when she found that Keith had set fire to a collection of cuddly toys he had loved. His teacher too was puzzled and worried by the relentless way in which Keith would suddenly destroy any small piece of work they had been able to do together. Despite daily personal attention from his class teacher and remedial teacher he was unable to begin to learn to read and remained in some profound sense untouchable.

When he could be controlled at school no longer he was referred again to the Tavistock. The school had struggled on with him for three years — a testimony, no doubt, to the good will and compassion of the teachers, but perhaps also to something in Keith himself, some quality which had inspired devotion in Miss A., which has kept him coming to his psychotherapy sessions for nearly five years with no absences due to anything other than illness.

responseSet.title: An Individual Approach to Psychotherapy with Psychotic Patients
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

An Individual Approach to Psychotherapy with Psychotic Patients

Eleonora D'ostiani

Eleonora D'ostiani

Via dei Sabelli 108
00185 Roma Italy

Eleonora D'ostiani  

When I look back over all the years I have worked with psychotic children, I realise how much of what I have learned has come from them and how they have patiently and perseveringly showed me the way to reach them, to understand them, and perhaps to help them. My patients have taught me to be humble: not to interpret but to listen, to have a dialogue where they “know” something I do not, something that I can only know if I approach them in a simple and open-minded manner. Until now I have not come very far along this road to knowledge and understanding. It promises to be long, but others may travel it faster and better than I. Perhaps I can share with them the errors and blind alleys which have blocked the way but which, when examined carefully, have shown themselves to be of inestimable help in understanding the reasons for failure.

Perhaps the first problem we face when dealing with a psychotic child is simply to understand him: he does not use language, or he uses an incomprehensible language, he is not in the habit of playing, he tends to act rather than feel and he seems to have an entirely different conception from ours of time, space and causality categories. This happens to both “shell” children and “entangled” children (Tustin, 1978). Thus it is not rare to experience the session as though it were a mass of bizarre, disconnected and confused acts or an accumulation of apparently unmotivated emotional reactions such as sudden escape, attacks, panic or anger.

Thus the report of a session with one of these patients can seem totally incomprehensible; for example: “…the child hit the plastic rings several times, walked on tiptoe to the window, then hit the window with the palm of his hand and then, after touching all the games laid on the table, went toward the door, shouting something incomprehensible…” How can you understand this sort of material? How can you keep from falling into the trap of understanding what you want to understand? And, most important of all, what does it mean to understand?

responseSet.title: How a Ten-Year-Old Girl Faced Her Death
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

How a Ten-Year-Old Girl Faced Her Death

P. Hinton

P. Hinton

London

P. Hinton  

This article attempts to describe the work of a medical social worker with a ten-year-old girl with terminal cancer. The work, which lasted a year, was mainly with the little girl herself. A language barrier made working with the parents difficult, though they, too, appeared to have been helped. My aim was to be as honest as possible with the child and to stay with her through the difficult time which lay ahead. Recognising her verbal and non-verbal communications, I followed her lead when she wished to talk about her fears or thoughts of death. Sometimes she needed to regress and be a very little girl; at others she was mature and competent. The essence of working with dying children depends on the worker's capacity to stay open to the full range of the child's experience, tolerating the pain, sharing the failures and triumphs, and not to lose sight of the fact of the child's imminent death.

Background Information

When Turia was referred to me, treatment of her cancer (Ewing's Sarcoma) with chemotherapy and radio-therapy had been started. Her parents brought her to see me weekly and I saw her more frequently when she was in hospital; these admissions occurred about every three weeks and the treatment consisted of an intravenous drip lasting twelve hours. The treatments caused multiple side-effects including nausea, vomiting and hair loss. Turia also had to undergo frequent laboratory investigations including repeated bone marrow aspirations.

Tuna's family, the K.'s, had come from Morocco three years previously; father was aged 38 and mother 36. There is one other child, a daughter aged five, who had been left with their maternal grandmother in Morocco until the parents established themselves enough to have both children in England. They had had one still birth, one son who died at the age of about one year, one daughter who died at six, and a son who died at twelve years. These children were severely handicapped. Turia denied any recollection of the death of her siblings although a sister had died when she was five and a brother when she was seven. Mr. K. had been a teacher in Morocco, but was a factory hand here. Mrs. K. had worked too, but she had stopped by the time I started seeing the family. Their financial and housing conditions were very poor.

responseSet.title: Adolescent Re-Enactment, Trauma and Reconstruction
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Adolescent Re-Enactment, Trauma and Reconstruction11

Margret Tonnesmann

Margret Tonnesmann

41a Aberdare Gardens
London, NW6 3AL

Margret Tonnesmann  

Ernest Jones, in his classical paper “Some Problems of Adolescence” (1922) speaks of the great changes that occur at the completion of adolescence and states, “At puberty a regression takes place in the direction of infancy,…and the person lives over again, though on another plane, the development he passed through in the first five years of his life”. Jones reasons that this is the key to many of the problems of adolescence “… it signifies that the individual recapitulates and expands in the second decennium of life the development he passed through during the first five years of life…” Moreover, Jones stresses that there is regression of “…other mental aspects than the purely sexual ones”. This paper was written before Freud introduced his structural theory in the “Ego and the Id” (1923). But I think we can nevertheless postulate that Jones already alluded to the regression of ego-functioning when he talked about those “other mental aspects”.

Adolescence has been for long the “step-child” of Psycho-analysis, as Anna Freud pointed out in 1958. Certainly, the names of such outstanding pioneers as Aichhorn, Bernfeld and Hoffer come to mind. But only over the last 20 years or so have psychoanalysts investigated the adolescent process more extensively, and its significance for the theory and practice of Psycho-analysis has become more evident.

The Normative Crisis of Adolescence

Adolescence is a developmental phase, a process which has a definite beginning with the onset of biological puberty and the re-organisation of the sexual instinct, and ends when the maturational processes have consolidated into what we call adulthood. Adolescence, the age between, is a normative crisis situation. It requires the relinquishment of the attachment to primary object(s) and incestuous figures and the modification of reliance upon parental ego-support and the parentally influenced ego-ideal and super-ego. It is a process of adaptation to adulthood in respect of hetero-sexual object-finding, self-object representation, ego synthesis, ego-ideal formation and super-ego restructuring. (Buxbaum ed., 1958; Blos, 1962; Erikson, 1956; Spiegel, 1951, 1958).

responseSet.title: Self-Observation, Insight, And the Development of “Knowing” in a Child Analysis
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Self-Observation, Insight, And the Development of “Knowing” in a Child Analysis

Ehud Koch

Ehud Koch

2040, Abington Road
Cleveland,
Ohio 44106
U.S.A.

Ehud Koch  

The case described in this paper was one of a series of cases examined with regard to the nature of self-observation and insight in the analyses of children. It was chosen for study because it involved a child who not only eschewed self-observation in the initial phases of treatment but also fought against gaining an understanding of herself. While defensive efforts at “not knowing” were greatly reduced by the end of her treatment, it was an open question whether she had achieved a significant understanding of herself; and whether such understanding (“insight”) as did occur figured in her remarkable advances in functioning. Thus, it seemed to be a useful case for considering such issues as: What is ‘insight’ in children? What forms does it take? What fosters its development? How relevant is self-understanding for ensuing psychological change?

An additional reason for this study was to attempt to understand why this child, so antagonistic to the treatment process, had done so well. While considerable understanding had been achieved regarding the nature and origins of her disturbance, much of which figured in the interpretive and reconstructive work of the analysis, it remained unclear, indeed mysterious, as to what specifically had promoted her impressive forward development. A “second look” at her treatment offered the chance to reconsider those particular elements that may have been the therapeutic agents of change.

This presentation is in three parts: (1) A brief background account of the symptom picture, developmental history, and salient issues as these were formulated at termination; (2) a tracing of those instances of self-observation that occurred in this analysis; and (3) some conclusions and hypotheses suggested by this study regarding the facilitation of the ego function of “knowing” and the development of insight.

In this paper the term “insight” refers to an integrative construction by the child of past and present experiences which represents a newly gained understanding of the self. While therapeutic interventions are understood as facilitating such understanding, insight itself is construed as a personal, creative achievement rather than as an assimilation of the therapist's understanding.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Two Regenerative Situations in Autism: Reclamation and Becoming Vertebrate

Anne Alvarez

Anne Alvarez

45, Flask Walk
London N.W.3

Anne Alvarez  

Introduction

For many years I have been working with an extremely ill and passive autistic boy named Bobbie whose inner world appeared to be perpetually empty. Where objects did exist, they were generally lifeless, useless and terribly fleeting; his sense of self was virtually non-existent. I found him exceptionally difficult to reach, partly because of inadequate treatment conditions, but largely because his withdrawal was so deep and chronic. When I began seeing him at the age of 7 he was far away and he had been so for a long time.

He is now 20. His development in treatment has been extremely slow and the developmental steps, though often initially dramatic, have been widely spaced, lingered over and dwelt upon in a way I shall describe later. However, this sluggishness itself has made it relatively easy to note the steps and the conditions which seemed to promote them. With less ill patients, or with normal infants, the pace of development is a great deal more rapid: thoughts, feelings, ambitions, achievements, checks, all flow together and across each other, often all at once. The complex eddies and currents move with such speed that it is not always easy to separate what is really new, or at least a renewal in a patient's development, from what may simply have gone unseen before.

Unfortunately for Bobbie, but fortunately for my ease in observing him, the repetitive pull and the pressure toward sameness means that real moves stand out in a striking way. It is also a fact that the facility with which he slipped away from contact and his excessive dependence on my contribution and efforts to contact him have led to a situation where I have had to examine much more closely than is usual the effect of my interpretations on his capacity for attention.

I shall describe two rather different situations in treatment which I think helped to bring him to life. I shall go on to suggest that these two situations may be closely related to certain maternal functions and to the acquisition of an internal object and a sense of self having at least the essential ingredients of human alive-ness. I shall illustrate these points further with brief material from two additional patients and from observations of four young babies.

responseSet.title: Psychotherapy with Severely Deprived Children: Introduction: The Tavistock Workshop

[[RunningHead]]

Psychotherapy with Severely Deprived Children: Introduction: The Tavistock Workshop

Mary Boston

Mary Boston

120, Belsize Lane
London N.W.3.

Mary Boston  

Severely deprived children have often been considered to be too emotionally damaged to be reachable by psychotherapy. Moreover, the practical difficulties of arranging regular attendance at a clinic for children who are “in Care” may seem insuperable. However, some attempts at treating severely deprived children have been published in previous issues of this journal (Boston, 1972; Newbolt, 1971; Henry, 1974). These cases suggested the possibility of a hopeful outcome, in spite of the difficulties experienced in the course of therapy.

In the Department for Children and Parents at the Tavistock Clinic, a gradually increasing number of children “in Care”, living in Children's Homes or in foster care, have in recent years been offered psychoanalytical psychotherapy. Keith and Eileen, described in the two papers which follow, are two of these children. As more such cases came into treatment in the department, a workshop was set up in order to study and review the experience gained. Twenty-two cases have so far been discussed. The sample was selected on the basis that the therapist be available and able to present the case for discussion at the workshop. It includes the majority of children “in Care” currently in psychotherapy in the Department for Children and Parents. (Five other children in psychotherapy have not so far been discussed because of unavailability of the therapist). Some parents who have experienced deprivation in childhood have also been presented. With the exception of one case, regular attendance in psychotherapy has been established with all the children and the patients seem to have been able to make considerable use of the opportunity. The frequency of sessions has varied from once to five times weekly. Most are still in treatment and have attended for longish periods of time.

Of course we do not know how representative of children in care these patients are. They may constitute a highly selected sample. It may be that there was something about these particular children that made them more likely to be referred for help. The reasons given for referral were in most cases to do with the pain and anxiety they evoked in others. Sometimes the behaviour complained of was alarming, or unbearable as with Eileen; sometimes it was appealing; sometimes there had been traumatic experiences. Very often the children were likeable, even if difficult, and thought to be capable of getting in touch with their feelings. It could be argued that they unconsciously sought help and that this was a hopeful sign.
